content: A halide is a binary chemical compound consisting of two parts: one is a halogen atom, and the other is an element or radical that is less electronegative than the halogen. This combination forms compounds such as fluorides, chlorides, bromides, iodides, or astatides. Many salts fall under the category of halides. All Group 1 metals react with halogens to form halides, which are typically white solids. A halide ion is a halogen atom that carries a negative charge. The halide anions include fluoride (F−), chloride (Cl−), bromide (Br−), iodide (I−), and astatide (At−). These ions are present in all ionic halide salts. In organic chemistry, halides are considered a functional group. Any organic compound containing a halogen atom is classified as a halide. Alkyl halides are a specific type of organic compound with the general formula R-X, where R represents an alkyl group and X represents a halogen atom covalently bonded to it. Pseudohalides are compounds that mimic halides in terms of charge and reactivity. Common examples of pseudohalides include azides (NNN−), isocyanates (−NCO), and cyanides (CN−). The Carius halogen method is a chemical test used to detect the presence of halogens in chemical substances. Metal halides are widely used in high-intensity discharge (HID) lamps, commonly referred to as metal halide lamps. Metal halide lamps are also utilized in greenhouses or regions with limited sunlight to supplement natural light. However, HID lamps, including metal halide lamps, contribute significantly to light pollution. Sodium-vapor lamps are often preferred in certain applications to mitigate this issue. Examples of halide compounds include: Sodium chloride (NaCl) Potassium chloride (KCl) Potassium iodide (KI) Lithium chloride (LiCl) Copper(II) chloride (CuCl₂) Chlorine fluoride (ClF) Bromomethane (CH₃Br) Iodoform (CHI₃) Silver chloride (AgCl)
